title: Devarim: the man of few words speaks (Deuteronomy 1:1)
hook: the one who said he was no man of words now speaks a whole book

segments.voice: Yesterday the last book of the Torah opened: Devarim, Moses' farewell. Your line was last words matter. Did you write your small goodbye to something? Today, a look at who is doing the talking. Day four hundred eighty-two.

Go back forty years, to a bush on fire in the desert. God tells a shepherd to go to Pharaoh, and the shepherd argues. In the old Jewish translation of Exodus he says, "I am not a man of words." He's slow of speech, he says, slow of tongue. Send someone else. God sends his brother Aaron along to do the talking. Now jump to the edge of the Jordan. The shepherd is an old man of a hundred and twenty. And the book that opens today is almost entirely him, talking. Speech after speech, for an entire book.
screen: `I AM NOT A MAN OF WORDS.` → `AARON DOES THE TALKING.` → `FORTY YEARS LATER: A WHOLE BOOK.`

segments.voice: The book begins: "These are the words which Moses spoke unto all Israel." In Hebrew, eleh ha-devarim. Devarim means words. The rabbis heard the irony right away. A midrash, in Deuteronomy Rabbah, sets the two verses side by side. At the bush, the Hebrew is lo ish devarim anochi, not a man of devarim. Here, eleh ha-devarim. The same word, forty years apart. Before, he couldn't speak. Now he speaks a whole book. What changed? The midrash's answer is that living with the Torah healed his tongue. Another way to hear it: forty years happened. He led a people who complained, he lost his sister and his brother, he broke tablets and carved new ones. Someone who has carried that much has something to say, and maybe stops worrying whether it comes out beautifully. And look at who he's speaking to: a generation that mostly wasn't there for the start of it, their parents having died in the wilderness. The man who once asked for someone else to do the talking is now the one who remembers out loud for everyone. He doesn't need to be polished. He needs to have been there. So the book of words belongs to the man who once had none. They didn't come from talent. They came from time.
screen: `THE MAN WHO SAID HE HAD NONE.` · `THE SAME WORD, FORTY YEARS APART.` · `TABLETS BROKEN, A SISTER AND BROTHER LOST.` · `THE ONE WHO REMEMBERS OUT LOUD.` · then, large: `WORDS COME WITH TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing you've been too shy to say. Settle, and breathe. Think of a meeting, a dinner table, a group chat where you usually stay quiet. Is there one thing you know, or think, or need, that you haven't said because you worry it will come out wrong? Let it form in your mind as a single plain sentence. Not eloquent. Just true. Say it to yourself a couple of times until it sounds like you. Then decide where today it could be said out loud. The bell holds the time.
Devarim. Words, or things spoken. The Hebrew name of Deuteronomy, from its opening line, these are the words.
Your line: words come with time. Today, speak up once, in a place where you'd normally stay quiet. Plain is fine. Day four hundred eighty-two.

screen: `DAY 482 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DEVARIM: SMALL AND GREAT ALIKE (DEUTERONOMY 1:17).`

howItsDone: Jewish communities begin reading Deuteronomy in the synagogue each summer with the portion Devarim, which is always read on the Sabbath just before Tisha B'Av.

original.note: Hebrew: words. what Moses said he lacked at the bush (Exodus 4:10), and the first key word of Deuteronomy.

trapdoor: what you thought: Deuteronomy is a book of extra laws.
what it means: devarim, words: Moses' farewell speeches, the journey retold by the man who once said he had no words.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 4:10 has lo ish devarim anochi, not a man of words; Deuteronomy 1:1 opens eleh ha-devarim; Deuteronomy Rabbah 1:1 reads them together.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the Greek name, Mishneh Torah and 'second telling' material that repeated day 481 (teach, match, myth, trapdoor) and replaced it with the same-word link between Exodus 4:10 and Deuteronomy 1:1; dropped the unsourced 'the way every book of the Torah does'; added Deuteronomy 31:2 as the source for Moses' age.
Deuteronomy 1:1 and Exodus 4:10 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify exact wording ('spoke unto all Israel'; 'I am not a man of words').
Deuteronomy Rabbah 1:1 contrasts Exodus 4:10 with Deuteronomy 1:1 and says the Torah healed Moses' speech; paraphrased, confirm the wording of the midrash's answer.
The name Mishneh Torah for Deuteronomy is rabbinic (from Deuteronomy 17:18); Greek Deuteronomion comes via the Septuagint's rendering of the same verse.
